 As we progress through a wet week, wind will also be a factor
 Flood Watch continues for Duval, St. Johns, Flagler, Clay & Putnam counties
 Katie Garner , The Morning Show Meteorologist , Jacksonville, FL 
 Published:  November 18, 2026 at 5:09 AM Updated:  November 18, 2026 at 7:17 AM Tags:  forecast , Weather We are heading into a significant, multi-day rainfall event across Northeast Florida and Southeast Georgia, with the greatest flooding concern focused along the Northeast Florida coast and St. Johns River basin through Friday night. 
 What makes this particular setup so concerning is the potential for multiple rounds of heavy rain to repeatedly impact the same communities, allowing rainfall totals to accumulate over several days.
 Here’s the meteorology behind this pattern. High pressure to our north is interacting with low pressure over the eastern and central Gulf of Mexico, while an inverted trough of low pressure develops along our Atlantic coastal waters. 
 The pressure gradient between these systems is maintaining persistent northeast to easterly winds, transporting abundant Atlantic moisture onshore. 
 Meanwhile, enhanced westerly flow higher in the atmosphere is working against the low-level easterly flow, supporting slow-moving and back-building showers, particularly along the Northeast Florida coastline. 
 Essentially, rainbands can continue developing and affecting the same areas, increasing our flash flooding potential.
 Today, the heavy rainfall and flash flooding risk increases, especially across St. Johns and Flagler counties. 
 The National Weather Service forecasts approximately 2–3 inches of rain across the Flood Watch area through tonight, with a 10% chance of exceeding 6 inches in some locations by 7 a.m. Thursday. 
 The Weather Prediction Center maintains a Level 2 of 4 Slight Risk for excessive rainfall today across the Flood Watch area and Southeast Georgia coast.
 Thursday, the strong upper-level ridge over the western Atlantic persists while the upper-level low moves northward toward the southern Appalachians. Surface high pressure shifts toward the Delmarva Peninsula, while Gulf low pressure and the coastal trough remain in place.
 The resulting pressure gradient maintains strong northeast winds of 15–25 mph, gusting to around 35 mph. Additional bands of heavy showers will push onshore, with isolated thunderstorms possible across southern portions of our area, including St. Johns, Flagler and Putnam counties.
 Friday brings another important development in this weather pattern. A strengthening southern-stream jet moves into the Gulf, reinvigorating the mid-level trough and supporting the development of a new surface low along a nearly stationary frontal boundary near South Florida. 
 This low is expected to lift north to northeast just offshore Friday afternoon and evening, organizing additional bands of heavy rainfall that could continue into early Saturday morning.
 The Weather Prediction Center has increased the excessive rainfall outlook to a Level 3 of 4 Moderate Risk Thursday for St. Johns and Flagler counties, expanding across the Northeast Florida coast Friday. 
 Rainfall totals of 4–8 inches are forecast across portions of Northeast Florida through Friday evening, with isolated totals of 8–12 inches possible. 
 The NWS Hydrology discussion also highlights the potential for localized amounts of 12 inches or more along the immediate coast where persistent, training rainbands develop. 
 Farther inland and along the Southeast Georgia coast, generally 2–4 inches are forecast, with isolated totals reaching 6–8 inches.
 A Flood Watch remains in effect through Friday evening for Duval, Clay, St. Johns, Putnam and Flagler counties. As rainfall continues, increasingly saturated soils and additional runoff will heighten flooding concerns. The St. Johns River and I-95 corridor through Duval County are also being monitored for potential river and small-stream flooding.
 Along the beaches, our persistent onshore flow will continue producing dangerous coastal conditions, including a high rip current risk, breaking waves of 7–10 feet and rough marine conditions. 
 High Surf Advisories and Small Craft Advisories remain in effect through Friday. Extensive cloud cover and repeated showers will also keep today’s temperatures below normal, with highs generally in the upper 60s to lower 70s.
 Improvement finally arrives Saturday as the developing surface low deepens and lifts northward through our coastal waters. The heaviest showers should gradually shift offshore, with inland rain chances decreasing throughout the day.
 Showers are expected to exit northeast by Saturday evening, followed by drier conditions Sunday. A weak cold front approaches Monday, but with limited forcing, rain chances remain low into early next week.
